title: How few real trials certify a robot policy when a biased simulator supplies the rest?
lede: research programme (milestone 3 done, 3d logged): valid, bias-agnostic sim-to-real evaluation of robot policies, consolidating about 130 twin projects into one question, with 13 checked references, hypotheses H1 to H6 and CoRL as the target venue
summary: An open research programme rather than a finished project. A digital twin is biased, so twin-only evaluation of a robot policy is wrong however many runs it makes; real trials are unbiased but scarce. The programme asks for estimators and tests that combine many twin runs with a few real ones, stay valid whatever the twin's bias, and say how many real trials they save, for mean return, failure rate and policy comparisons. It reconciles two answers already in this repository: control-variate savings that grow as 1/(1−ρ²) (twin-evaluation) and a worst-case result that a twin cannot shorten a failure-rate certificate (twin-certification). Planned: one estimator family under context pairing (control variate, PPI++, multifidelity Monte Carlo), a certification lower bound under checkable discrepancy assumptions, active choice of real trials, anytime-valid stopping, and tests on MuJoCo model pairs and on SIMPLER's published paired real and simulated results. First results (milestone 3, 21 MuJoCo model-versus-model pairs): context-paired twin runs raise the effective real sample up to 3.2×, within 6% of 1/(1−ρ²(1−n/N)); unpaired twin runs give none; plug-in t intervals undercover (as low as 87% at n=30; real-only reaches 91%) so H1 is refuted as pre-registered; detectability predicts value almost as well as ρ here (Spearman −0.95 vs 0.999). Magnitudes of the omitted effects are swept, not sourced from datasheets. Milestone 3b: a studentised-bootstrap interval lifts mean 95% coverage at n=30 from 92.0% to 93.6% for the control variate (worst pair 90.8%) at 14% greater mean width, while the percentile bootstrap is worse than the t interval; a distribution-free interval is still needed for a guarantee. Milestone 3c: a union-bound empirical-Bernstein interval for the control variate is valid (100% coverage on all 21 pairs) but 2.1–3.1× wider than a real-only one, because the bound is dominated by its range term; the twin's variance gain is invisible to it, which rules out generic Bernstein bounds and points to betting or observed-range intervals. Milestone 3d: a betting (hedged-capital) interval is also valid (coverage at least 99.5%) and again 1.9–3.4× wider with the twin, because its bets are capped on 99–100% of steps, so any bound that leans on the worst-case range hides the twin's variance gain at n=30–60.
